items.stem: Define the term "proportional representation".
items.answer: An electoral system giving parties seats in proportion to votes, which in Weimar Germany produced many small parties and unstable coalitions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an electoral system giving parties seats in proportion to votes, which in Weimar Germany produced many small parties and unstable coalitions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Weimar Germany was a failure from the start." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It survived the crises of 1919–23 and enjoyed relative stability and cultural achievement in 1924–29 under Stresemann.
items.markingKey: It survived the crises of 1919–23 and enjoyed relative stability and cultural achievement in 1924–29 under Stresemann. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the hyperinflation of 1923 and the Depression of 1929–33.
items.answer: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment.
items.markingKey: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A class brainstorm on the interwar crisis: the Great Depression and the weakness of new democracies produced the question "What was the Depression?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How far did US loan recalls after 1929 cause the rise in German unemployment between 1929 and 1932?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How far did US loan recalls after 1929 cause the rise in German unemployment between 1929 and 1932?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the Great Depression hit Germany especially hard.
items.answer: German recovery depended on US loans under the Dawes Plan; after 1929 these loans were recalled, causing bank failures, collapsing industry and mass unemployment.
items.markingKey: Content: German recovery depended on US loans under the Dawes Plan; after 1929 these loans were recalled, causing bank failures, collapsing industry and mass unemployment. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Economic history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Charles P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, Berkeley, 1973

The historian argued that the world depression was so deep and long because no country was willing or able to act as a stabiliser: Britain no longer could and the United States would not, so no one kept markets open, provided loans or acted as a lender of last resort.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating the interwar crisis: the Great Depression and the weakness of new democracies.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Charles P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, Berkeley, 1973. Purpose: to explain the causes and duration of the Depression. Value: It is an influential analysis by a leading economic historian. Limitation: It focuses on international leadership and gives less weight to domestic policies such as the gold standard.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Charles P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, Berkeley, 1973. Purpose: to explain the causes and duration of the Depression. Value: It is an influential analysis by a leading economic historian. Limitation: It focuses on international leadership and gives less weight to domestic policies such as the gold standard. Award up to [4]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: The exchange rate was about 493.2 marks per US dollar in July 1922 and about 98,860,000 marks per dollar in September 1923. By what factor did the number of marks per dollar increase?
items.answer: about 200,446 times
items.markingKey: 98,860,000 ÷ 493.2 = 200,446.1 (M1 A1). Approximate historical rates.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "The Great Depression was the main reason for the collapse of democracy in Germany."
items.answer: Thesis: The Depression was the essential trigger, but structural weaknesses and the decisions of conservative elites explain why democracy collapsed rather than survived as in Britain or the USA.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: unemployment of 6 million drove voters to the Nazis and Communists; the Nazi vote jumped from 2.6% in 1928 to 37% in July 1932. Counter-arguments: the constitution's weaknesses, such as Article 48 and PR, made government unstable; elite politicians such as von Papen chose to bring Hitler into power. Thesis/conclusion: The Depression was the essential trigger, but structural weaknesses and the decisions of conservative elites explain why democracy collapsed rather than survived as in Britain or the USA. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Explain why protectionism deepened the Depression.
items.answer: When countries raised tariffs to protect their industries, others retaliated, so world trade collapsed and export industries lost markets, increasing unemployment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When countries raised tariffs to protect their industries, others retaliated, so world trade collapsed and export industries lost markets, increasing unemployment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the hyperinflation of 1923 and the Depression of 1929–33.
items.answer: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment.
items.markingKey: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Brüning's deflationary policies as an example, explain the weakening of parliamentary democracy.
items.answer: Chancellor Heinrich Brüning (1930–32) cut spending and wages using Article 48 decrees; unemployment kept rising. Rule by decree made democracy seem irrelevant and austerity deepened the crisis.
items.markingKey: Context (Chancellor Heinrich Brüning (1930–32) cut spending and wages using Article 48 decrees; unemployment kept rising.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: rule by decree made democracy seem irrelevant and austerity deepened the crisis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the weakening of parliamentary democracy.

items.stem: Which of these is a feature shared by fascist and communist states in the 1930s?
options: Private ownership as the core economic belief of both
A single-party state using censorship and secret police
items.answer: A single-party state using censorship and secret police
items.markingKey: D. Both were totalitarian in practice.

items.stem: A student claims: "Fascism and Nazism are exactly the same." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Nazism was a form of fascism, but its racial antisemitic ideology was more central and extreme than in Italian Fascism, at least before 1938.
items.markingKey: Nazism was a form of fascism, but its racial antisemitic ideology was more central and extreme than in Italian Fascism, at least before 1938. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why liberal democracy was under pressure in the 1930s.
items.answer: Economic depression, fear of communism, nationalist grievances and the apparent success of dictatorships made many people doubt that democratic governments could solve crises. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Economic depression, fear of communism, nationalist grievances and the apparent success of dictatorships made many people doubt that democratic governments could solve crises. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Czechoslovakia in the interwar years as an example, explain democratic survival.
items.answer: Under President Tomáš Masaryk, Czechoslovakia remained a parliamentary democracy until 1938 despite economic and minority tensions. It shows that democracy could survive in new states created in 1918.
items.markingKey: Context (Under President Tomáš Masaryk, Czechoslovakia remained a parliamentary democracy until 1938 despite economic and minority tensions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows that democracy could survive in new states created in 1918. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to democratic survival.

items.stem: On a timeline, the Spanish Civil War begins is marked at 1936 CE and Germany annexes Austria (Anschluss) at 1938 CE. Calculate the number of years between the two events.
items.answer: 2 years
items.markingKey: 2 by subtraction (M1 A1). BCE years count down towards 1 BCE; the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on political ideologies: democracy, communism, fascism and Nazism produced the question "What is fascism?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How did Mussolini consolidate his power in Italy between 1922 and 1926?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How did Mussolini consolidate his power in Italy between 1922 and 1926?" items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An authoritarian, ultra-nationalist ideology emphasising a single leader, one party, militarism and the subordination of the individual to the state; first in power in Italy under Mussolini"?
items.answer: fascism
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of fascism.

items.stem: Place these events in chronological order, earliest first: Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany (1933 CE); The Communist Manifesto is published (1848 CE); Mussolini bans opposition parties (1926 CE); the USSR is formed (1922 CE).
items.answer: The Communist Manifesto is published → the USSR is formed → Mussolini bans opposition parties → Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany
items.markingKey: The Communist Manifesto is published → the USSR is formed → Mussolini bans opposition parties → Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany. A larger BCE number is earlier. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark one adjacent pair swapped.

items.stem:
Source A – Political writing (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto, London, 1848

The authors argued that the history of all existing society is the history of class struggles, and that the working class would overthrow capitalism and create a society without classes, in which the means of production would be owned in common.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Communism and fascism had more in common than their ideologies suggest."
items.answer: In methods of rule they were similar, which is why many historians use "totalitarianism"; in aims and economic organisation they differed greatly.
items.markingKey: From the source: Class struggle drives history and workers will create a classless society. Own knowledge for: both created single-party states with a leader cult, secret police and propaganda; both sought to control the economy and society. Own knowledge against: their goals differed fundamentally: class equality versus national/racial hierarchy; their economic systems differed: collective ownership versus private business under state direction. Judgement: In methods of rule they were similar, which is why many historians use "totalitarianism"; in aims and economic organisation they differed greatly. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "propaganda"?
options: The severe worldwide economic slump that followed the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 and lasted through the 1930s
A term for a relatively prosperous peasant; "dekulakisation" targeted millions for deportation or death
The mass repression of 1936–38, including show trials and about 680,000 recorded executions
Information, often biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view
items.answer: Information, often biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view
items.markingKey: D. "propaganda" is information, often biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view.

items.stem: Explain why the Nazis gained support between 1929 and 1932.
items.answer: The Depression created mass unemployment and fear; the Nazis offered strong leadership, jobs and national revival, used modern propaganda and blamed scapegoats, appealing to many groups.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Depression created mass unemployment and fear; the Nazis offered strong leadership, jobs and national revival, used modern propaganda and blamed scapegoats, appealing to many groups. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between consent and coercion.
items.answer: Consent is support given willingly, for example due to jobs or propaganda; coercion is obedience forced by fear and repression.
items.markingKey: Consent is support given willingly, for example due to jobs or propaganda; coercion is obedience forced by fear and repression. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: How many years passed between the Nuremberg Laws (1935 CE) and the Berlin Olympics (1936 CE)?
items.answer: 1 years
items.markingKey: 1 by subtraction (M1 A1). BCE years count down towards 1 BCE; the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE.

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Ian Kershaw, The "Hitler Myth": Image and Reality in the Third Reich, Oxford, 1987

The historian argued that Hitler's power rested heavily on a "Hitler myth" – an image of a leader above party politics who embodied the nation – created by propaganda and sustained by foreign policy successes, and that it declined as the war turned against Germany.

According to Source A, what can we learn about the rise of Hitler and Nazi Germany: methods and propaganda? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: Propaganda created an image of Hitler that underpinned the regime's popularity.
items.markingKey: Propaganda created an image of Hitler that underpinned the regime's popularity. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why the Enabling Act was important for Hitler.
items.answer: It allowed his government to make laws without the Reichstag, giving a legal appearance to dictatorship and enabling him to ban parties and trade unions.
items.markingKey: Content: It allowed his government to make laws without the Reichstag, giving a legal appearance to dictatorship and enabling him to ban parties and trade unions. items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How effective was Nazi radio propaganda in shaping public opinion in Germany between 1933 and 1939?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use radio ownership data, SOPADE reports and two historians; evaluate sources; reach a judgement; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use radio ownership data, SOPADE reports and two historians; evaluate sources; reach a judgement; cite in MLA. items.stem: Explain why the Night of the Long Knives strengthened Hitler's position.
items.answer: It removed SA leaders such as Röhm who threatened the army's support, eliminated other rivals and showed that Hitler would use violence, securing the army's backing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It removed SA leaders such as Röhm who threatened the army's support, eliminated other rivals and showed that Hitler would use violence, securing the army's backing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Hitler seized power in a violent revolution in 1933." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: He was appointed legally by President Hindenburg after conservative politicians believed they could control him; the dictatorship was then built step by step.
items.markingKey: He was appointed legally by President Hindenburg after conservative politicians believed they could control him; the dictatorship was then built step by step. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Place these events in chronological order, earliest first: the Nazis become the largest party in the Reichstag (1932 CE); Hitler is appointed chancellor and the Enabling Act passes (1933 CE); the Berlin Olympics (1936 CE); Kristallnacht (1938 CE).
items.answer: the Nazis become the largest party in the Reichstag → Hitler is appointed chancellor and the Enabling Act passes → the Berlin Olympics → Kristallnacht
items.markingKey: the Nazis become the largest party in the Reichstag → Hitler is appointed chancellor and the Enabling Act passes → the Berlin Olympics → Kristallnacht. A larger BCE number is earlier. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark one adjacent pair swapped.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Holodomor"?
options: The mass repression of 1936–38, including show trials and about 680,000 recorded executions
The clause of the Weimar constitution allowing the president to rule by emergency decree
The man-made famine in Ukraine in 1932–33, caused by collectivisation and grain requisitioning, in which millions died
Government by a ruler or small group that is not accountable to the people and restricts political freedom
items.answer: The man-made famine in Ukraine in 1932–33, caused by collectivisation and grain requisitioning, in which millions died
items.markingKey: C. "Holodomor" is the man-made famine in Ukraine in 1932–33, caused by collectivisation and grain requisitioning, in which millions died.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Stalin introduced collectivisation.
items.answer: He wanted to secure grain to feed the cities and to export to pay for industrial machinery, to control the peasantry and to eliminate private farming.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: He wanted to secure grain to feed the cities and to export to pay for industrial machinery, to control the peasantry and to eliminate private farming. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the achievements of the Five-Year Plans and their human costs.
items.answer: Industrial output, especially coal, steel and electricity, rose rapidly; but this was achieved through forced labour, low living standards, famine and repression.
items.markingKey: Industrial output, especially coal, steel and electricity, rose rapidly; but this was achieved through forced labour, low living standards, famine and repression. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Collectivisation increased food production immediately." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Grain output and especially livestock numbers fell sharply in the early 1930s.
items.markingKey: Grain output and especially livestock numbers fell sharply in the early 1930s. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sana is investigating Stalin's USSR: collectivisation, the Five-Year Plans and the Terror and proposes the research question: "Was Stalin bad?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a vague value question Improved: "How far did collectivisation achieve Stalin's aims for Soviet agriculture between 1929 and 1939?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a vague value question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How far did collectivisation achieve Stalin's aims for Soviet agriculture between 1929 and 1939?" items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Joseph Stalin, speech to the First All-Union Conference of Leading Personnel of Socialist Industry, Moscow, 4 February 1931

The leader told industrial managers that the USSR was fifty to a hundred years behind the advanced countries and must make good the distance in ten years, or it would be crushed.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Stalin's economic policies were a success."
items.answer: In industrial and military terms they achieved much, but at an enormous human cost; whether this counts as success depends on the criteria used.
items.markingKey: From the source: The USSR had to industrialise rapidly to survive. Own knowledge for: industrial output grew rapidly and the USSR could fight and win the Second World War; new cities, factories and dams were built. Own knowledge against: collectivisation caused famine with millions of deaths; living standards fell and growth relied on forced labour. Judgement: In industrial and military terms they achieved much, but at an enormous human cost; whether this counts as success depends on the criteria used. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The Soviet state planning committee that set economic targets"?
items.answer: Gosplan
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Gosplan.

items.stem: With reference to the Moscow show trials, explain how it illustrates the Great Terror.
items.answer: Between 1936 and 1938 leading Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed to invented crimes and were executed. Public trials spread fear and eliminated potential rivals.
items.markingKey: Context (Between 1936 and 1938 leading Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed to invented crimes and were executed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: public trials spread fear and eliminated potential rivals. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the Great Terror.

items.stem: Official Soviet statistics show steel output rising from 4.0 million tonnes (1928) to 17.7 million tonnes (1937). Calculate the percentage increase, and evaluate how far historians can rely on these figures as evidence of the success of the Five-Year Plans.
items.markingKey: (17.7 − 4.0) ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 342% (M1 A1). Evaluation (4): official figures were produced to show success and managers inflated output to meet targets; quality was often poor; Western estimates are lower but still show rapid growth; consumer goods and human costs are not shown.

items.stem: About how many Germans were unemployed by early 1932?
items.answer: About 6 million
items.markingKey: A. Roughly a third of the workforce.

items.stem: In the July 1932 Reichstag election, about what share of the vote did the Nazis win?
items.answer: About 37%
items.markingKey: A. It made them the largest party.

items.stem: Define the term "liberal democracy".
items.answer: A political system with free elections, the rule of law, protection of individual rights and peaceful transfer of power
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a political system with free elections, the rule of law, protection of individual rights and peaceful transfer of power. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a market economy and a command economy.
items.answer: In a command economy the state owns industry and sets output and prices; in a market economy private firms respond to prices set by supply and demand.
items.markingKey: In a command economy the state owns industry and sets output and prices; in a market economy private firms respond to prices set by supply and demand. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Depression weakened support for democracy in Europe.
items.answer: Mass unemployment and poverty made people lose faith in democratic governments that seemed unable to act, so extremist parties promising strong leadership gained support.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mass unemployment and poverty made people lose faith in democratic governments that seemed unable to act, so extremist parties promising strong leadership gained support. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between terror and propaganda.
items.answer: Propaganda sought to persuade people to support the regime; terror (Gestapo, SS, camps) sought to frighten people into obedience.
items.markingKey: Propaganda sought to persuade people to support the regime; terror (Gestapo, SS, camps) sought to frighten people into obedience. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between communism and fascism.
items.answer: Communism is internationalist, aims at a classless society and collective ownership; fascism is ultra-nationalist, accepts private property under state direction and glorifies the nation and leader.
items.markingKey: Communism is internationalist, aims at a classless society and collective ownership; fascism is ultra-nationalist, accepts private property under state direction and glorifies the nation and leader. items.markingKey: Award marks for: He wanted to secure grain to feed the cities and to export to pay for industrial machinery, to control the peasantry and to eliminate private farming. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "The Wall Street Crash alone caused the Great Depression." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The crash was a trigger; overproduction, weak banks, debt, the gold standard and protectionism turned it into a global depression.
items.markingKey: The crash was a trigger; overproduction, weak banks, debt, the gold standard and protectionism turned it into a global depression. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In the Reichstag election of September 1930 the Nazi party won 107 of 577 seats. Calculate its share of seats as a percentage, and compare it with its vote share of 18.3%.
items.answer: 18.5% of seats, close to its 18.3% vote share

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Ian Kershaw, The "Hitler Myth": Image and Reality in the Third Reich, Oxford, 1987

The historian argued that Hitler's power rested heavily on a "Hitler myth" – an image of a leader above party politics who embodied the nation – created by propaganda and sustained by foreign policy successes, and that it declined as the war turned against Germany.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the rise of Hitler and Nazi Germany: methods and propaganda. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Ian Kershaw, The "Hitler Myth": Image and Reality in the Third Reich, Oxford, 1987. Purpose: to analyse popular opinion and the role of propaganda in the Third Reich. Value: It uses reports on public opinion from many sources. Limitation: Public opinion in a dictatorship is hard to measure, so conclusions are partly interpretive.

items.stem: In which century did Mussolini bans opposition parties (1926 CE) take place?
items.answer: 20th century CE
items.markingKey: B. 1926 CE falls in the 20th century CE: e.g. the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How far did collectivisation achieve Stalin's aims for Soviet agriculture between 1929 and 1939?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use grain and livestock statistics, Stalin's speeches and two historians; compare aims and outcomes; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use grain and livestock statistics, Stalin's speeches and two historians; compare aims and outcomes; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How far did US loan recalls after 1929 cause the rise in German unemployment between 1929 and 1932?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use German unemployment statistics, loan data and two historians; graph trends; weigh other causes; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use German unemployment statistics, loan data and two historians; graph trends; weigh other causes; cite in MLA. items.stem: "Propaganda was more important than terror in maintaining Nazi control of Germany." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Historians such as Ian Kershaw argue that consent and coercion worked together: propaganda won many, while terror targeted those who would not conform.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: propaganda created the Hitler myth and genuine popularity among many; economic recovery and full employment, publicised by propaganda, won support. Arguments against: the Gestapo, camps and informers crushed opposition; fear of denunciation silenced critics. Supported judgement: Historians such as Ian Kershaw argue that consent and coercion worked together: propaganda won many, while terror targeted those who would not conform. The authors argued that the history of all existing society is the history of class struggles, and that the working class would overthrow capitalism and create a society without classes, in which the means of production would be owned in common.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching political ideologies: democracy, communism, fascism and Nazism? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto, London, 1848. Purpose: to set out the aims of the Communist League and rally workers. Value: It is the foundational statement of communist ideology. Limitation: It is a political pamphlet, not a description of how communist states actually operated in the 20th century.

items.stem: "Stalin's economic policies were a success." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: In industrial and military terms they achieved much, but at an enormous human cost; whether this counts as success depends on the criteria used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: industrial output grew rapidly and the USSR could fight and win the Second World War; new cities, factories and dams were built. Arguments against: collectivisation caused famine with millions of deaths; living standards fell and growth relied on forced labour. Supported judgement: In industrial and military terms they achieved much, but at an enormous human cost; whether this counts as success depends on the criteria used. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929"?
items.answer: Wall Street Crash
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Wall Street Crash.

items.stem: Define the term "Volksgemeinschaft".
items.answer: The Nazi idea of a "people's community" united by race and loyalty, which excluded those the regime defined as outsiders
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the Nazi idea of a "people's community" united by race and loyalty, which excluded those the regime defined as outsiders. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "liberal democracy"?
options: A political system with free elections, the rule of law, protection of individual rights and peaceful transfer of power
Information, often biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view
A system in which a single party seeks total control over every aspect of public and private life
A centrally planned programme setting production targets for industry; the first ran from 1928
items.answer: A political system with free elections, the rule of law, protection of individual rights and peaceful transfer of power
items.markingKey: A. "liberal democracy" is a political system with free elections, the rule of law, protection of individual rights and peaceful transfer of power.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Collectivisation increased food production immediately." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Grain output and especially livestock numbers fell sharply in the early 1930s.
items.markingKey: Grain output and especially livestock numbers fell sharply in the early 1930s. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Depression of 1929–33 and the hyperinflation of 1923.
items.answer: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment.
items.markingKey: Hyperinflation in 1923 destroyed savings through rapidly rising prices; the Depression brought falling prices, collapsing output and mass unemployment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Hitler seized power in a violent revolution in 1933." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: He was appointed legally by President Hindenburg after conservative politicians believed they could control him; the dictatorship was then built step by step.
items.markingKey: He was appointed legally by President Hindenburg after conservative politicians believed they could control him; the dictatorship was then built step by step. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between fascism and communism.
items.answer: Communism is internationalist, aims at a classless society and collective ownership; fascism is ultra-nationalist, accepts private property under state direction and glorifies the nation and leader.
items.markingKey: Communism is internationalist, aims at a classless society and collective ownership; fascism is ultra-nationalist, accepts private property under state direction and glorifies the nation and leader. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a command economy and a market economy.
items.answer: In a command economy the state owns industry and sets output and prices; in a market economy private firms respond to prices set by supply and demand.
items.markingKey: In a command economy the state owns industry and sets output and prices; in a market economy private firms respond to prices set by supply and demand. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Great Depression hit Germany especially hard.
items.answer: German recovery depended on US loans under the Dawes Plan; after 1929 these loans were recalled, causing bank failures, collapsing industry and mass unemployment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: German recovery depended on US loans under the Dawes Plan; after 1929 these loans were recalled, causing bank failures, collapsing industry and mass unemployment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the Hitler Youth and explain what it reveals about control of society.
items.answer: Membership became compulsory in 1936 (enforced from 1939); by 1939 it had about 8 million members. The regime aimed to shape young people's beliefs and loyalty.

Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Joseph Stalin, speech to the First All-Union Conference of Leading Personnel of Socialist Industry, Moscow, 4 February 1931

The leader told industrial managers that the USSR was fifty to a hundred years behind the advanced countries and must make good the distance in ten years, or it would be crushed.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into Stalin's USSR: collectivisation, the Five-Year Plans and the Terror, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Joseph Stalin, speech to the First All-Union Conference of Leading Personnel of Socialist Industry, Moscow, 4 February 1931. Limitation: It is a public speech designed to motivate; it ignores the costs and his own political motives.

items.stem:
Source A – Economic history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Charles P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, Berkeley, 1973

The historian argued that the world depression was so deep and long because no country was willing or able to act as a stabiliser: Britain no longer could and the United States would not, so no one kept markets open, provided loans or acted as a lender of last resort.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The Great Depression was the main reason for the collapse of democracy in Germany."
items.answer: The Depression was the essential trigger, but structural weaknesses and the decisions of conservative elites explain why democracy collapsed rather than survived as in Britain or the USA.
items.markingKey: From the source: The Depression was deep because there was no international leader to stabilise the economy. Own knowledge for: unemployment of 6 million drove voters to the Nazis and Communists; the Nazi vote jumped from 2.6% in 1928 to 37% in July 1932. Own knowledge against: the constitution's weaknesses, such as Article 48 and PR, made government unstable; elite politicians such as von Papen chose to bring Hitler into power. Judgement: The Depression was the essential trigger, but structural weaknesses and the decisions of conservative elites explain why democracy collapsed rather than survived as in Britain or the USA. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Communism and fascism had more in common than their ideologies suggest."
items.answer: In methods of rule they were similar, which is why many historians use "totalitarianism"; in aims and economic organisation they differed greatly.

Supported judgement: In methods of rule they were similar, which is why many historians use "totalitarianism"; in aims and economic organisation they differed greatly.
